sections.name: The signs are still readable
sections.intro:
You're back. Before anything else — a walk through the old neighbourhood, taking stock of what survived the rusty year.

Ground rules: this diagnostic is built to be too hard to finish — the top of every section is deliberately out of reach, and a skip is data, not defeat. Do it in short sittings; your work saves automatically and will be here when you return. You'll need a Russian keyboard enabled for some answers (Settings → Keyboard — and yes, typing Cyrillic is part of the job you're training for). Spelling with е for ё is always accepted. No punctuation needed anywhere.

questions.prompt: Off the plane, into the city. Read the signs — answer in English.

parts.label: «БАНК»
parts._working: БАНК = bank. Pure decoding of friendly letters (Б А Н К all near-Latin or familiar). Opens with guaranteed wins — the section measures rust in reading speed, not knowledge.

parts.label: «МЕТРО»
parts._working: МЕТРО = metro. All English equivalents accepted (subway/underground/tube).

parts.label: «КАФЕ»
parts._working: КАФЕ = café. Accent and plain-e variants both listed — the engine does not normalise accents, so café ≠ cafe as strings.

parts.label: «ТАКСИ»
parts._working: ТАКСИ = taxi. Four-for-four here = alphabet fully intact; hesitation shows up later in the harder letters, not these.

questions.prompt: Now the letters that betray tourists — the false friends and the genuinely Cyrillic ones.

parts.label: «РЕСТОРАН»
parts._working: РЕСТОРАН = restaurant. Р=R and С=S are the classic false friends; reading this fluently means the Latin-lookalike trap is long dead. English misspellings of 'restaurant' accepted — English orthography is not under test.

parts.label: «ВЫХОД»
parts._working: ВЫХОД = exit/way out. Contains ы and х — no Latin crutches at all, and it's THE survival sign. A miss here is a real (small) gap, not rust.

parts.label: «ЦЕНТР»
parts._working: ЦЕНТР = centre. Ц is unguessable from Latin; otherwise near-cognate. UK and US spellings both accepted.

parts.label: «ВОКЗАЛ»
parts._working: ВОКЗАЛ = (railway) station — famously derived from London's Vauxhall. Not decodable: you either know it or you don't, which makes it the bridge from script-reading into vocabulary proper. Expected hit for someone who lived there two years.

questions.prompt: Reverse gear — and a keyboard check. Type these INTO Cyrillic. (If your Russian keyboard isn't set up yet, do it now; the rest of the walk needs it.)

parts.label: internet →
parts._working: интернет. Doubles as the Cyrillic-keyboard shakedown before the grammar sections demand it. One canonical spelling; anything else → review (a human can tell a typo from a gap).

parts.label: vodka →
parts._working: водка. Second keyboard rep, zero vocabulary load, and the first wink at the bar thread of this course.

sections.name: People — meeting and knowing them
sections.intro: The whole point of the return: the people. This section maps the vocabulary of getting to know someone.

questions.prompt: Into English:

parts.label: «друг»
parts._working: друг = friend. Core A1; the anchor word of the course's social thread.

parts.label: «работа»
parts._working: работа = work/job. Both English senses accepted. The business thread's anchor word.

parts.label: «город»
parts._working: город = city/town (covers both English words; Russian doesn't split them at A1).

parts.label: «дом»
parts._working: дом = house/home (and colloquially an apartment block). All senses accepted.

questions.prompt: Warmer now — the words conversations are made of:

parts.label: «встреча»
parts._working: встреча = meeting (social or business — both live in this course; 'date' and 'appointment' accepted as context-dependent readings).

parts.label: «сосед»
parts._working: сосед = neighbour. UK/US spellings. The Return's courtyard world makes this one load-bearing later.

parts.label: «разговор»
parts._working: разговор = conversation/talk. The course's stated goal is literally this word — worth knowing on day zero whether it's already in stock.

parts.label: «вопрос»
parts._working: вопрос = question (also 'issue/matter' in business register — accepted).

questions.prompt: Into Russian (Cyrillic, dictionary form is fine):

parts.label: friend →
parts._working: друг (подруга female, приятель looser, друзья plural — all accepted; the question tests retrieval, not which register he reaches for).

parts.label: name →
parts._working: имя (a person's name). название (a thing's name) accepted at diagnostic stage — the distinction is itself a nice future teaching point, and reaching for either shows retrieval.

parts.label: to meet / get to know someone →
parts._working: познакомиться (get acquainted) is the target; знакомиться (imperfective), встретить(ся)/встречаться (to meet up) all accepted — the знакомиться/встретиться distinction is exactly the kind of nuance the course will teach, so any of the family counts today. Misspelled -тся/-ться variants accepted (that trap bites natives).

questions.prompt: Top of the people ramp — the nuance shelf. Into English:

parts.label: «знакомый» (as a noun: мой знакомый)
parts._working: знакомый = acquaintance — the person between stranger and друг. B1 because the word's force is relational nuance, not dictionary lookup. A hit means the social-register ladder survived the rust.

parts.label: «собеседник»
accept: the person you are talking to
the other person in a conversation
parts._working: собеседник = interlocutor/conversation partner. Deliberately near the ceiling; it's also quietly the course's mascot word — the thing Timothy wants to BE in a bar.

parts.label: «общаться»
parts._working: общаться = to socialise/communicate/spend time talking with people. No single English equivalent — hence the wide accept list; any of the senses shows the word is alive.

sections.name: The bar and the street
sections.intro: Friday night vocabulary. This is where the course is ultimately headed, so let's see today's stock.

questions.prompt: Into English:

parts.label: «пиво»
parts._working: пиво = beer. If any word survived two years in Russia, it's this one.

parts.label: «вино»
parts._working: вино = wine. Near-cognate (vino).

parts.label: «счёт»
parts._working: счёт = the bill (in a bar), also 'account' in business Russian — both accepted, and the double meaning is a future bridge between the bar thread and the business thread. Shown with ё; he answers in English so the ё/е issue doesn't arise here.

parts.label: «улица»
parts._working: улица = street ('on улица' idiomatically = outside, accepted).

questions.prompt: Getting around and getting served:

parts.label: «заказать»
parts._working: заказать = to order (food/drink) or book (a table/taxi) — both senses accepted. The single most useful bar verb.

parts.label: «рядом»
parts._working: рядом = nearby/next to. High-frequency spatial word; Dima uses it in the reading section («бар рядом с офисом») — a deliberate plant so section 6 rewards section 3.

parts.label: «налево»
parts._working: налево = (to the) left. Directions vocabulary — street navigation strand.

parts.label: «ещё»
parts._working: ещё = more/another/still/yet — famously context-dependent; ANY of its senses accepted. In a bar it means 'another one', which is why it's in this section.

questions.prompt: Your round. Into Russian (Cyrillic):

parts.label: beer →
parts._working: пиво. Production counterpart of v3q1a — recognising and retrieving are different muscles, and the gap between them is a key diagnostic readout for a rusty speaker (recognition usually survives; retrieval rusts first).

parts.label: please →
parts._working: пожалуйста. The misspelling пожалуста (dropped й) is extremely common even among learners who SAY it perfectly — accepted, since what's tested is retrieval of the word, not its orthography. Anything else → review.

parts.label: the bill, please →
parts._working: счёт, пожалуйста — with е-for-ё variants (the engine treats ё and е as different characters, so both spellings are listed for every ё word) and comma/no-comma variants (punctuation is NOT stripped by normText). можно счёт / принесите счёт are more idiomatic upgrades — accepted with extra credit noted at review.

questions.prompt: Top shelf. Into English:

parts.label: «двор»
parts._working: двор = courtyard — THE unit of Russian urban social life, and the planned setting of this course's first unit. B1 as vocabulary; a hit means he lived in one, which is better than any textbook.

parts.label: «здание»
parts._working: здание = building. Neutral B1 filler on the ramp — included so the top of this strand isn't all culture-loaded words.

parts.label: «закуска»
parts._working: закуска = the food that accompanies drinks — appetiser/starter/bar snack all accepted, plus the loanword 'zakuski'. Culturally load-bearing for the bar thread (drinking without закуска is practically illegal).

sections.name: Cases — the old enemy
sections.intro: You said the grammar broke you. Let's map exactly where it broke — ending by ending. Type ONLY the missing word (the dictionary form is in brackets). е for ё is fine; expect the top of this page to be out of reach.

questions.prompt: Where you live. «Я живу в ____ (Москва)»

parts.label: the missing word
parts._working: в + prepositional: Москва → Москве (-а → -е). The first case every learner meets and the one most likely to have survived. Diagnostic of: baseline case machinery present at all.

questions.prompt: Where you're heading, and who you spot there.

parts.label: «Я иду в ____ (бар)»
parts._working: в + accusative of direction: бар is masculine inanimate, so accusative = nominative — the word does NOT change. Knowing when NOT to decline is real knowledge; a learner who writes баре here is applying the location case to a direction (the classic в+prep/в+acc confusion, worth catching early).

parts.label: «Я вижу ____ (Анна)»
parts._working: Accusative of a feminine animate: Анна → Анну (-а → -у). Pairs with part a to test whether accusative is understood as a system (changes here, doesn't change there) rather than a memorised ending.

questions.prompt: The genitive earns its keep: of-phrases and not-having.

parts.label: «бутылка ____ (вино)»
parts._working: Genitive after a quantity word: вино → вина (-о → -а). 'A bottle OF wine' — the genitive's friendliest job, and bar-relevant.

parts.label: «У меня нет ____ (работа)»
parts._working: нет + genitive: работа → работы (-а → -ы). 'I don't have a job' — thematically pointed for a returner job-hunting in the city. нет-genitive is the construction learners report hating most; its presence/absence here steers the whole grammar unit order.

questions.prompt: Dative and instrumental — the cases that rust first.

parts.label: «Я звоню ____ (друг)»
parts._working: звонить + dative: друг → другу. 'I'm calling my friend' — social thread. Dative after звонить/помогать/говорить is a B1 reflex; rust shows here before it shows in prep/acc.

parts.label: «Я работаю ____ (архитектор)»
parts._working: работать + instrumental for profession: архитектор → архитектором (-ом). Chosen because it is literally the sentence Timothy will say in every Russian introduction for the rest of his life — 'I work as an architect.' If exactly one ending from this page gets drilled into permanence, it should be this one.

questions.prompt: The wall itself: genitive plural, where every learner's confidence goes to die.

parts.label: «пять ____ (друг)»
parts._working: Numbers 5+ take genitive plural: друг → друзей (irregular stem друз- + -ей). Deliberately brutal: irregular plural AND gen-pl in one word. A hit here would genuinely surprise and would move the grammar ceiling up a band.

parts.label: «много ____ (люди)»
parts._working: много + genitive plural: люди → людей. 'Many people' — unavoidable in any conversation about a party, a bar, a company. Suppletive plural (человек/люди) makes it a fair B1+ ceiling marker.

questions.prompt: Full agreement, two words at once: «Мы говорим о ____ ____ (новая работа)» — about the new job.

parts.label: both missing words
parts._working: о + prepositional with adjective agreement: новая работа → (о) новой работе — adjective -ая → -ой, noun -а → -е, both at once. Adjective–noun agreement under a case is the B1+ summit of this strand; partial credit (one of two endings right) is visible at review since the raw answer is stored. The redundant о-included variant is accepted (people retype the preposition).

sections.name: Verbs — getting things moving
sections.intro: Conjugation, past tense, verbs of motion, and the famous aspect problem. Where a choice is offered in brackets, type the one that fits.

questions.prompt: Present tense, first person and third:

parts.label: «Я ____ (работать) в Москве»
parts._working: работать → я работаю (1st conjugation, -ю). Baseline conjugation check.

parts.label: «Она ____ (говорить) по-русски»
parts._working: говорить → она говорит (2nd conjugation, -ит). Covers the other conjugation class, so the two parts together test whether the two-conjugation system itself is intact.

questions.prompt: Last night. «Вчера я ____ (быть) в баре»

parts.label: the missing word
parts._working: Past tense of быть, masculine: был. была also accepted (the gender-agreement slip is a different, smaller error than failing to form the past at all — the review read distinguishes them; the raw answer is stored either way).

questions.prompt: Verbs of motion — walking or riding?

parts.label: «Сейчас я ____ на работу пешком (иду / еду)»
parts._working: On foot (пешком), right now → идти: иду. The иду/еду split is foot vs vehicle. Note the frame is 'сейчас' (right now, one direction) deliberately — a habitual frame like 'every day' would demand the multidirectional хожу, which is a different lesson and would make the question unfair as a binary choice.

parts.label: «Завтра я ____ в Петербург на поезде (иду / еду)»
parts._working: By train (на поезде) → ехать: еду. (Present tense for a planned trip tomorrow is idiomatic Russian, like English 'tomorrow I'm going'.) Together with part a: does the foot/vehicle axis survive? It's the gateway to the whole motion-verb system, a flagged B1 nightmare that the course must sequence carefully.

questions.prompt: Aspect — the one that broke you. Pick the verb that fits.

parts.label: «Вчера я наконец ____ эту книгу (читал / прочитал)»
parts._working: наконец (finally) signals completion → perfective: прочитал. THE diagnostic aspect question: 'finally' forces the perfective, no ambiguity. Feminine form accepted (as v5q2).

parts.label: «Я ____ письмо два часа (писал / написал)»
parts._working: Duration (два часа, for two hours) forces the imperfective: писал. Mirror image of part a — the pair tests whether aspect is understood as completion-vs-process rather than guessed. Both right = the concept survived; both wrong or inconsistent = aspect gets its own unit, early.

questions.prompt: Future, perfective flavour: «Когда я закончу, я ____ тебе (позвоню / звоню)»

parts.label: the verb that fits
parts._working: 'When I finish, I'll call you' — one-off future action → perfective future: позвоню. The bare present звоню cannot carry this meaning after an explicit когда-clause. Tests whether perfective-present-form = future is understood — a structural B1 insight, not vocabulary.

questions.prompt: The summit: unreal mood. «Если бы у меня было время, я ____ с тобой (пойти)» — if I had time, I'd go with you.

parts.label: the missing words
parts._working: Conditional: past form + бы → пошёл бы. Accepted: е-for-ё spellings (standing rule), either word order (both грамотный), feminine forms (as v5q2). Deliberately out of reach — if he nails the conditional cold after a rusty year, the course's grammar ceiling moves from B1 to B2 and the plan changes.

sections.name: A message from Dima
sections.intro: Your phone buzzes. It's Dima — an old friend from the first time round. Read it all, then answer in English. The message starts easy and gets harder: that's the ramp.

questions.prompt:
Привет! Это Дима. Ты правда снова в Москве? Отлично!

Я теперь работаю в компании, которая делает платформу для данных.

Работа интересная, но времени всегда мало.

В пятницу после работы мы идём в бар рядом с офисом.

Приходи — познакомлю тебя с коллегами.

Если не сможешь в пятницу, напиши, когда тебе удобно.

First pass, easy ones:

parts.label: Who wrote the message?
parts._working: Это Дима = It's Dima. Name-spotting across scripts; answer accepted in either script.

parts.label: Where does he suggest meeting?
parts._working: мы идём в бар = we're going to a bar. A1: бар is known from section 3 (deliberate plant). Location detail (near the office) optional — any bar-shaped answer lands.

questions.prompt: Second pass:

parts.label: When is the bar trip?
parts._working: В пятницу после работы = on Friday after work. пятница (Friday) + после работы (after work) — either or both accepted. A2 time expressions.

parts.label: What does Dima's company make?
parts._working: компании, которая делает платформу для данных = a company that makes a data platform. платформа is a cognate; данные (data) is the key unlock — and the word Timothy's entire professional life orbits, planted here to test whether his own field's Russian vocabulary is in stock. (It also quietly announces the course's business setting.)

questions.prompt: Third pass — between the lines:

parts.label: What does he complain about?
parts._working: времени всегда мало = there's always too little time. Requires parsing времени (genitive of время after мало) — a case form doing semantic work. B1 reading: the grammar IS the meaning here.

parts.label: What does he promise to do at the bar?
accept: to introduce me to his colleagues
parts._working: познакомлю тебя с коллегами = I'll introduce you to my colleagues. Perfective future of знакомиться's transitive sibling + instrumental plural — but the VOCAB was planted in v2q3c, so a reader can crack it from the known stem знаком-. Tests exactly that: leveraging a known root to read an unknown form. Wide accept list; paraphrases land at review.

questions.prompt: Last line, hardest line: «Если не сможешь в пятницу, напиши, когда тебе удобно.» What is Dima asking you to do, exactly?

parts.label: if Friday doesn't work, you should…
accept: write and say when is good for you
message him when you are free
parts._working: Если не сможешь… напиши, когда тебе удобно = If you can't make Friday, write (to say) when suits you. Stacked B1+ machinery: conditional clause, perfective future сможешь, imperative напиши, dative idiom тебе удобно. The accept list catches the main paraphrase shapes; most real answers will land at review and be read for the three content points (condition + write + convenient time).

sections.name: Your turn to speak — on paper
sections.intro: Production. First two have exact answers; the last two are free writing — a human (or a well-briefed AI) reads those, the engine won't try. Cyrillic throughout.

questions.prompt: Say: “I lived in Moscow.”

parts.label: in Russian
parts._working: Я жил в Москве — past tense + в + prepositional, the autobiographical sentence he'll say in every introduction. Accepts: dropped я (natural speech), жила (gender slip, logged as minor at review), and the в России variant in case he generalises the place. Spelling of Москве must be exact-ish — but близко misses land at review, not wrong.

questions.prompt: Say: “I want to speak Russian.”

parts.label: in Russian
parts._working: Я хочу говорить по-русски — хотеть + infinitive + the по-русски adverbial. Accepts hyphen, space and run-together spellings of по-русски (the engine strips spaces but NOT hyphens, so each variant must be listed explicitly), and the dropped-я form. The mission statement of the entire course, in his own typing.

questions.prompt: Now reply to Dima, in Russian: say yes to Friday, and ask him one question about his company. Two or three sentences. Don't polish — write like you'd text.

parts.label: your reply to Dima
parts._working: Free writing, no accept list → textarea, marks as 'review' by design (capturing free writing without pretending to mark it — the engine's documented mechanism). The rubric reads it for: communicative success first (would Dima understand?), then case/aspect control, then range. The question-about-the-company half elicits an interrogative + probably a prepositional (о компании / о работе) without saying so.

questions.prompt: Friday came. Dima waves you over: «Это мой друг из Англии!» Introduce yourself to the table: name, where you're from, what you do for work, one thing about your history with Russia. Three or four sentences, in Russian.

parts.label: your introduction
parts._working: Free writing → review. The canonical self-introduction — the single most reusable paragraph in his future. Elicits: имя constructions, из + genitive (origin), работаю + instrumental (profession — planted in v4q4b), and a past-tense biography line (жил, planted in v7q1). The rubric compares what he produces here against which of those planted forms he got right upstream: same grammar, scored vs spontaneous — the truest picture of what's actually usable.

sections.name: Debrief — back at the hotel
sections.intro: The walk is done. Now the part that steers everything: honest notes. Nothing here is marked.

questions.prompt: Score each section for enjoyment — 1 (chore) to 5 (genuinely fun):

parts.label: The signs (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, script strand. Range 1–5, any value correct — survey, not test. Per the Playbook these drive tailoring as much as scores: high-skill/low-joy strands get deferred and re-entered through an interest; low-skill/high-joy strands lead.

parts.label: People words (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, people-vocabulary strand.

parts.label: The bar and the street (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, bar/city-vocabulary strand.

parts.label: Cases (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, cases strand. The one to watch: he reports grammar broke him — if enjoyment here is ≥3 despite low scores, the appetite for a direct assault on cases exists; if 1–2, cases get smuggled in through usage instead.

parts.label: Verbs and aspect (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, verbs strand. Same read as cases.

parts.label: Dima's message (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, reading strand. His reading was historically his strength — expect high; if ALSO high joy, reading becomes the course's engine room.

parts.label: Writing back (1–5)
parts._working: Enjoyment rating, production strand.

questions.prompt: Which question was your favourite, and why?

parts.label: favourite question
parts._working: Free text → review. Playbook survey staple; self-named favourites reveal the hook the course should hang difficulty on.

questions.prompt: What do you actually remember most fondly about speaking Russian in Russia? Be specific — a place, a person, a phrase, a night.

parts.label: the fond memory
parts._working: Free text → review. The Return's emotional fuel tank. Whatever he names becomes course material: a remembered bar becomes the bar, a remembered person becomes an NPC alongside Dima. Motivation harvesting, verbatim.

questions.prompt: What exactly broke you last time? Name names — the construction, the situation, the moment you switched to English.

parts.label: what broke
parts._working: Free text → review. Self-diagnosis to triangulate against the measured cases/aspect results. Where self-report and measurement agree, that's Unit 1 or 2; where they disagree (he fears something he actually scores fine on), that's a confidence problem, not a knowledge problem — different treatment.

questions.prompt: Name three topics you'd genuinely want to hold forth on in a bar — in any language. (These become the conversation targets.)

parts.label: three topics
parts._working: Free text → review. Sets the B-level conversation syllabus: the course builds topic-specific vocabulary lanes toward exactly these, since 'comfortable conversation about relatively complex topics' is the stated goal and comfort is topic-dependent. Expect data/architecture to appear; don't assume it.
